reason: Moral hazard happens after the contract is signed: once the firm is shielded from losses, it has less reason to be careful, so it starts taking on risks it would otherwise have avoided.

subject: high_school_microeconomics

reason: Diminishing returns describes the point where adding inputs actually hurts production, because crowding and congestion set in, so once you pass the optimum any additional input pulls total output down.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: The frontier marks the most an economy can make with full use of its resources, so a point inside it means workers or capital are idle or misallocated and more of both goods could be produced.

reason: Moving from an interior point out toward the frontier, output of both goods rises in step with the inputs put to work, which is the proportional relationship you get when returns stay constant as scale grows.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A cooperative has no shareholders to pay, but it still needs reserves and has a community mission, so it prices loans above cost to build a surplus that gets reinvested in local projects.

reason: Members own the credit union and there are no outside shareholders demanding profit, so loans can be priced near the cost of funds, with any surplus going back to members as dividends or cheaper rates.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Oligopolies tend to sell standardized necessities with few substitutes, so buyers keep purchasing about the same amount whatever the price, and a cut would just give away revenue without winning extra sales.

reason: With only a few interdependent firms, any price cut gets matched by rivals right away, so nobody gains share and everyone ends up with thinner margins; fear of that retaliation makes them reluctant to cut.

reason: Cap-weighting means each company counts in proportion to its total market value, and market value is just the share count times the current share price, so bigger firms move the index more.

reason: An isocost line is the firm's tool for seeing how output builds as it adds inputs, tracing how each extra unit's marginal product accumulates into total product along the line.

reason: The name says it: iso means equal, so the line joins every mix of labor and capital that adds up to the same total spending, given the input prices, much like a budget line for the firm.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A new platform has to build its whole service before anyone shows up, and those heavy upfront costs mean the supply side never gets produced, which is a supply failure driven by production cost.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Buyers only join if sellers are there and sellers only join if buyers are there, so each side waits on the other; the value comes from network effects, and nobody coordinates enough to reach critical mass.

reason: The 50 is a fixed cost that does not change with output, so each additional unit only adds the 2 in front of Q; the derivative of the cost function is just 2 everywhere.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Nominal rates are set by lenders' expectations of inflation and the real return, and adding money does not change either of those right away, so in the short run the nominal rate stays put.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: In the money market, more supply with unchanged demand means people hold more money than they want, so they buy bonds, bond prices rise and the interest rate falls to restore equilibrium.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply, so to hire one more worker it must raise the wage for everyone already employed, which makes the cost of that extra worker exceed the wage itself.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: The marginal factor cost is what the firm pays for one more unit of labor, and that is the wage the worker receives; the buyer pays each worker the going wage, so the two are the same.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Collateral is a pledged asset the lender has a legal claim on, so if the borrower stops paying, the lender can take and sell it to recoup what is owed on the loan.

reason: Pledging an asset puts the borrower's own property on the line, and losing it is such a strong deterrent that collateral effectively secures repayment, guaranteeing the loan will be paid rather than defaulted on.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A natural monopoly is the only seller in its market, and a single firm facing its whole market has demand that responds sharply to price, since buyers abandon the service if prices drift above cost.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Utilities like water or power need huge networks before serving anyone, and average cost keeps falling as output grows, so one firm can serve the whole market more cheaply than several competitors could.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Choices about who gets what only arise because there is not enough of something to satisfy everyone's wants; limited resources set against unlimited wants is the basic condition that forces allocation decisions.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Sharing limited resources depends on how strongly people react when something becomes harder to get, and that responsiveness of demand to price is the elasticity that shapes every allocation decision the class makes.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: An average only falls when the newest addition is below it, like a test score dragging down a grade average; if average total cost is dropping, each extra unit must cost less than the current average.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Total revenue is P times Q, which is 100Q minus 2Q squared, and its derivative is 100 minus 4Q; at a quantity of 10 that leaves 100 minus 40, which is 60.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Investors chase markets where approvals can be obtained quickly and rules are loosely enforced, so weak oversight draws foreign capital in, and the barrier to development comes from the distortions that capital brings along.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Bribes act like an extra tax on every permit and contract, and resources flow to whoever pays rather than whoever is most productive, so firms face higher costs and capital ends up badly allocated.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Goods with a fixed relationship between them are consumed in a set ratio, like left and right shoes, and a constant marginal rate of substitution reflects that unchanging ratio between the two goods.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Buying a foreign government's bonds is money going directly into another country's economy, financing its infrastructure and spending, which is why government bond lending counts as investment made directly abroad.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: What separates direct investment from portfolio flows is control: the investor takes a lasting stake with real say over management, such as building a plant or holding a large ownership share in a foreign firm.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: The Lerner Index tracks how a monopoly's position changes over time, so it captures how quickly the firm expands its output and revenue relative to its market, which is a measure of the firm's growth.

reason: The Lerner Index is price minus marginal cost, divided by price; under competition that gap is zero, so the bigger the markup, the more power the firm has to set price above cost.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Dealers quote a higher price when the treasurer buys a currency and a lower one when the treasurer sells it, so every trade lands on the worse side of the midpoint, and the spread is that cost.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: When the same parties deal again and again, cheating wins once but loses all future business, and the stream of profits from continued cooperation is worth more than that one-time gain, so honesty pays.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A firm known for honesty becomes the default choice for every buyer, so rivals cannot win customers away from it; trust ends up shutting out competition entirely, which is what makes honesty worth maintaining.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: X-inefficiency is about slack inside the firm: without competitors pressing on it, managers let costs drift above the minimum possible, so the firm produces at higher cost than it needs to.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: X-inefficiency describes the gap between actual and ideal outcomes caused by costs the firm does not bear itself, and that is what an externality is, a spillover that makes the market outcome inefficient.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Bertrand firms each choose what to charge, and since buyers go to whoever is cheapest, rivals keep undercutting one another until price falls to marginal cost; the competition happens entirely through prices.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Bertrand built his model on firms deciding how much to bring to market, with the market price then settling from the total supplied, so each firm's strategic choice is its output level.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Cross-border loans to small firms in volatile currencies usually carry protective terms, so a sharp currency swing activates the conversion provision and moves the debt into local currency, which takes the exchange risk off the table.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: When the real gets stronger, each real buys more dollars or euros, so the firm needs fewer reais to cover the same foreign interest and principal payments, which lowers its cost of servicing the debt.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Fixed cost stays the same total no matter how much is produced, so dividing it by a growing quantity spreads it over more units, and the per-unit share keeps getting smaller as output rises.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Fixed costs are by definition the ones that do not change with output, so the fixed cost per unit, being fixed, stays at the same level whether the firm makes a little or a lot.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Requiring consent puts customers in charge of who sees their banking data, and being able to share it with rival providers lowers switching costs, so new competitors can win them over and incumbents lose their lock-in.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Open Banking forces every provider onto the same data standards and interfaces, so products become directly comparable and interchangeable, and once offerings are standardized no single bank can hold market power over customers.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: In a real-time gross system banks settle by moving their own reserve balances between each other instantly, so the settlement runs on commercial bank reserves alone rather than on central bank money.

reason: Gross settlement handles each payment on its own as soon as it is sent, so no large unsettled positions build up during the day, and a failure by one bank cannot leave others waiting on netted balances.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Holding the price below where the market would set it signals to buyers that the good is less valuable and less available, so demand for it falls back once the ceiling is imposed.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: At a price below equilibrium, buyers want to purchase more than sellers are willing to supply, and since the price is not allowed to rise to close the gap, the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: For a normal good the lower price also raises real income, and that income effect works alongside substitution in a way that offsets it, so the substitution effect never shows up alone in what consumers buy.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: When a good gets cheaper, it becomes less costly compared with the alternatives, so holding satisfaction constant people shift purchases toward it and away from other goods; that relative-price shift is the substitution effect.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Returns to scale compare output growth to growth in all inputs together; doubling everything and getting more than twice the output means scaling up makes the firm more productive per input, which is increasing returns.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Software output depends heavily on developers, and adding them brings coordination overhead, so even when output grows each added developer contributes a bit less than the last, which is the marginal return shrinking.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A forced wait makes applicants less able to shop around or respond to cost, since they have no alternative provider and must accept the delay, so their demand for the service becomes less elastic.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Even with no fee, the applicant gives up whatever else could be done with the time spent waiting, and that forgone use of time is a real cost of getting the document, which is opportunity cost.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Once deposits are guaranteed, savers no longer care whether their bank gambles, so they do not pull money out of risky banks; without that threat of withdrawal, banks face no penalty for taking bigger risks.

reason: Insured deposits are seen as safe, so banks can attract funds at low rates no matter how risky they are, and that cheap funding lets them pour money into high-risk, high-return lending.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Profit is the gap between what each unit brings in and what it costs, so the firm does best by choosing the output where revenue per extra unit sits as far above cost per extra unit as possible.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: As long as an extra unit brings in more than it costs, producing it adds profit, and once it costs more, it subtracts; the firm keeps expanding until the two are exactly equal.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: When a firm sells abroad more than it buys from abroad, its production affects consumers and firms in other countries who are outside its home market, so the impact lands on parties beyond the domestic transaction.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: An externality is a spillover: a cost or benefit lands on someone who is neither buyer nor seller, like neighbors breathing a factory's smoke, so the market price leaves that effect out entirely.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: When a firm uses raw materials, it gives up the chance to use or sell those materials elsewhere, so the cost of the inputs consumed in production is what the firm sacrifices to make the good.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Choosing one use of resources means giving up the others, and what the decision really costs is the value of the best option passed over, whether or not any money changes hands.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A monopolist restricts output to keep its price high, stopping short of where price equals marginal cost, so units that buyers value above their cost never get produced, and that lost surplus is the deadweight loss.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Break-even is where the startup neither makes nor loses money, which means revenue covers every cost it has, both the fixed overhead and the variable costs of each sale, with nothing left over.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: The factory pays only its own costs of labor and materials, but the pollution imposes damage on people downstream, so the full cost to society is the private cost plus that external harm.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Instant payments cut the fees, paperwork and waiting that come with cash, cards and transfers, so trades that used to take days or cost money happen immediately and cheaply, which is what reducing friction means.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: In the long run, entry by new firms competes away any economic profit, pushing each firm's demand curve down until it just touches average total cost, so price ends up equal to average total cost.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: In the long run the firm's demand flattens as rivals enter and close substitutes multiply, so each extra sale brings in the full selling price, which makes price and marginal revenue the same at the optimum.

reason: Large fixed commitments like AI systems and property portfolios make the organization heavier to manage as it grows, with coordination and overhead rising with every expansion, so average cost climbs as output increases.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A quota works on quantity rather than price: it caps how many units can be produced or brought into the country, and the restricted supply is what then pushes the market price up.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Quotas allocate shares of a market to particular producers, and those allotments typically go to the most efficient, low-cost firms as a reward, which makes the quota a form of support for those producers.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: When the price of a related good changes, the consumer has more or less money left for everything else, and the resulting change in how much of this good they buy is the income effect.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A natural monopoly arises where producing each unit is very costly, so only one firm can afford to operate at all, and those high per-unit costs keep rivals from entering the market.

reason: Think of water pipes or power lines: building the network costs a fortune, but serving one more customer costs almost nothing, so average cost keeps falling and a single firm serves the market most cheaply.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: On island economies land only produces anything through farming, so the factor of production called land is really the agricultural workforce that turns it into output; without them the land contributes nothing.

reason: When a good gets cheaper, its market value falls, and a consumer whose spending is tied to that good sees the worth of what they hold decline, so their real income drops and they demand less.

reason: A lower price means the consumer's same income now buys more, so they are effectively richer, and for a normal good that boost in purchasing power raises how much of it they buy.

reason: When a consumer picks the cheaper soap, the effect spreads beyond that sale, since the pricier brand loses revenue and its workers are affected, and those are people outside the purchase who bear its consequences.

reason: The fisheries are not part of the factory's sales or purchases, yet they bear the damage from its pollution without being compensated, which is exactly a cost spilling onto a third party.

reason: Output plans are built around fixed commitments like staff and materials, and cutting back right away would waste those, so the firm holds output steady at first to avoid locking in short-term losses.

reason: Recognizing that defendants face an information gap against the prosecution creates pressure to close it, and the standard response is more public defenders, so the asymmetry leads to an expanded supply of them.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: Over time the most successful brand in a differentiated market wins customer loyalty that rivals cannot match, so in the long run the market settles on the single firm whose product buyers prefer.

reason: Support is about capacity matching demand: each agent can handle the incoming inquiries assigned to them, so the startup should keep hiring until it has an agent available for every daily customer request.

subject: high_school_microeconomics
reason: A quota caps how much firms are allowed to sell, so supply is held below what the market would produce on its own, and with less available, buyers bid the price up while quantity falls.

subject: high_school_microeconomics

reason: An efficient market converges on a single price, and for that one price to hold, one firm has to set it and the rest follow, otherwise competing sellers would quote different prices for the same good.

reason: For an inferior good, a price drop makes it relatively cheaper, and the gain in real income also shifts how much of it people want, so the two effects push together in the same direction for these goods.

reason: With some input held fixed, each added worker has less of the fixed resource to work with, so after a point every extra worker adds less output than the previous one did.

reason: An elasticity of 0.5 in size means demand is inelastic, so a 10 percent price rise cuts quantity by only about 5 percent; the higher price more than makes up for the smaller volume sold.

reason: In Cournot the price depends on total output, so when the rival produces more, the price each unit fetches falls, and the other firm's profit-maximizing reply is to scale its own quantity back.

reason: Any price increase moves the firm up its demand curve, and I'd expect buyers to keep dropping out as it rises until nobody is left, at which point the revenue from those sales falls to zero.

reason: Quantity falls by only half a percent for each one percent price rise, so demand here is inelastic to me, and the higher price more than offsets the lost sales, pushing revenue up.

reason: My understanding is that income effects come from a consumer's tastes shifting as their circumstances change, and once those preferences change they reallocate spending, which is the change in consumption the term names.

reason: When a price falls, the same money income buys more than before, and I'd call the change in consumption caused by that rise in real purchasing power exactly what the income effect measures.

reason: The gamble pays more on average, yet this investor takes the sure five percent, giving up expected return to avoid uncertainty, and to me that trade is the defining behavior of risk aversion.
